title: Sessions
intro.1: One session is one Chrome, its screen, its sound, and the agent that drives it.
starting-a-session.title: Starting a session
starting-a-session.4: Fit this device by default: a size real desktops have (1440x900, 1920x1080…), of your screen’s shape and near your window’s width, drawn scaled to your window. Or pick a size.
starting-a-session.6: Off by default. On, Chrome’s debugging endpoint listens inside the session, which the agent’s run_javascript needs. Sites may notice it. See The agent.
starting-a-session.8: Leave directly, or through one of the proxies added under Proxies, checked before the session starts. The browser then takes that egress’s time zone and languages.
starting-a-session.10: Off by default: a fresh browser that keeps nothing. On, the session keeps what this browser saves (logins, site data, history, preferences; not its caches), encrypted, and brings it back when you resume it (see Persistent sessions below).
starting-a-session.11: A new session opens on Google; over the API it opens the url you give it (https://, or http://, which Chrome tries over HTTPS first; a site without HTTPS does not open). An agent’s session takes the installation’s screen size (ADMIN_OUTPUT). The time zone and languages are the installation’s (ADMIN_TIMEZONE, ADMIN_LANGUAGES), or, for a session that leaves through an egress, that egress’s. What a session allows (typing and clicking, copy and paste, files, sound, recording) is set as it starts and can’t be changed afterward.
control.title: Control
control.1: One viewer at a time holds the control lease; only its input reaches the browser. Taking control first pauses the agent’s calls and proves none still runs (see The agent); giving it back lets the agent act again.
control.2: Closing the tab, losing the connection or logging out gives control back.
timeline.title: What happened while you were away
timeline.1: Each session keeps a timeline: what its agent did and how each action went, the pages it was on, who held control and why it changed, the files it saved or sent, and the questions it asked you. The Timeline button in the session’s bar opens it with the session’s replay; when your agent has worked since you left, the button says how much and opens at the first new event, with what is new summed up.
timeline.2: It keeps what the agent did, never what it typed: a click and the control it named, how many characters it typed, the keys of a shortcut, a script as a script, and whether each action went through, not what a tool said when it failed. File names are scrubbed of what you typed, as the agent’s answers are. A page’s title is kept as the screen shows it, and not while you have control.
timeline.3: Filter it to the agent, to people, or to what went wrong, and download it as Markdown (an agent can follow it) or JSON. The admin’s API serves it too: GET /api/sessions/{id}/timeline.
timeline.4: A session that stopped keeps its timeline under Past sessions in Sessions, so you can read what happened in one your agent stopped; Forget deletes it now.
timeline.5: Up to 2,000 events a session, the oldest going first. They are kept encrypted on the server’s disk with the replay, and outlast a restart; a session that was running then keeps what was last written, up to a minute old.
timeline.6: Each action says who made it: a token by its name, an agent on this server, or your page. An agent’s request for you shows with what it wrote, and how it closed.
replay.title: Replay
replay.1: While your agent has control, the session records its screen. The replay plays it beside the timeline’s events, each one a line (point at it for all it says) and a place to jump to; with nothing recorded, the events show alone.
replay.2: Play, pause, go from event to event, and play at 0.5×, 1×, 2×, 4× or 8×; Skip idle time (on by default) jumps over the stretches where nothing changes. The position bar marks every event, problems in red, and shades what was not recorded.
replay.3: It records nothing while a person has control: it stops before your input reaches the page and starts again, from a whole picture, once the agent has control again. It is a video of the whole screen, made to follow what happened rather than to match every pixel, and a screen that stays still adds almost nothing; the replay needs a browser that plays AV1. Settings sets its picture size and sharpness (75% and Low unless you change them) for what is recorded from then on, and says about what they take.
replay.4: Recordings and timelines stay encrypted on the server’s disk. After a restart, only your password opens them: until you enter it (a passkey sign-in does not), they stay locked under Past sessions. A password set anew, after the old one was lost, opens none of them, and they are deleted. A session records even with nobody signed in. Settings sets the share of the whole disk they may take, 10% unless you change it, and they never leave less than 1 GiB free. Past the limit, whichever session holds the most loses its oldest part, cut where a whole picture starts, so one heavy session eats its own past and the others keep theirs; when each holds only its last part, the session stopped longest ago goes.
replay.5: Record what the agent does, on by default, is one of the switches a session starts with; the public demo records nothing.
chat.title: Chat with your agent
chat.1: From a session’s bar, open your own Claude Code or Codex in a terminal over the screen, at the bottom or as a sidebar. It works in this session’s browser alone, over MCP, with no agent token and whatever a saved session’s list of agents says. Hide it and it keeps running; it keeps running with the tab closed too, until its program exits or the session stops.
chat.2: Add one account for each login you want to use, several of each program, identified by its email. Each has a home of its own on the server, which holds the program, its login and its conversations. A session has one chat at most, and an account can be open in several sessions at once, each chat working in its own session’s browser alone. They share that home, its conversations and the account’s usage limits, like several terminals on one computer. easi.run never switches accounts by itself, and each maker’s terms apply to your accounts.
chat.3: The first time an account opens, the program comes from its maker’s own installer, unmodified (up to about 650 MB), and you sign in inside the terminal, by the program’s own flow. For Codex on a remote server, pick the device code, which you first turn on in ChatGPT’s security settings. easi.run never reads that home; unlike a saved session it is not encrypted with your password, so anyone who can run Docker on the server can read it.
chat.4: While you hold control, its actions in the browser are refused, as any agent’s are; opening the chat gives control back if you hold it. Once you give it back, the chat sees the screen again: unlike other agents, it receives screenshots after a takeover. They go to that account’s provider and can show what you did in the session. In what it reads as text, what you typed is still removed.
chat.5: It runs in a container of its own, whose only way out is a proxy of its own to public addresses on port 443, not the session’s proxy. It may use 2 CPUs and 1 GiB of memory beyond what the number of sessions at once counts, and what the home keeps stays on the server’s disk until you remove the account.
keyboard-and-clipboard.title: Keyboard and clipboard
keyboard-and-clipboard.1: Text travels as text, so what you type does not depend on the server’s keyboard layout.
keyboard-and-clipboard.2: Paste with your usual shortcut: your clipboard’s text goes to the page.
keyboard-and-clipboard.3: Copy on the page while you hold control: the text goes to your clipboard, as it would in your own Chrome. Where your browser does not allow that, a button puts it there.
keyboard-and-clipboard.4: On a Mac, Command acts as Control in the remote browser, so ⌘C, ⌘V and ⌘A work as you expect, and Option with an arrow, Backspace or Delete acts as Control too, for word moves and word deletes.
files-and-downloads.title: Files and downloads
files-and-downloads.1: Upload: when the page opens a file chooser, your own file picker opens; or drag files onto the screen.
files-and-downloads.2: Download: the page’s downloads stream to your own browser’s Downloads, byte for byte. A page saved with Chrome’s Save as arrives whole, as one MHTML file.
recording.title: Recording
recording.1: Whoever holds control can record the session: press Record, pick a microphone and a camera (or none), the camera’s corner radius, and whether to include the page’s sound. The camera is a square: drag it to place it, and drag its corner handle to resize it.
recording.2: The display records the screen itself, at its own resolution: AV1 video at 30 frames a second (10 Mbit/s) and Opus sound at 128 kbit/s, in a .webm file.
recording.3: Your camera and microphone are sent to the server while it records, and drawn and mixed into the video there.
recording.4: The file streams to your Downloads as it is made, and is complete when you stop. One recording at a time, up to an hour or 8 GiB. Giving control away or closing the tab ends it.
sound.title: Sound
sound.1: The page’s sound plays in your browser, with mute and volume controls. Browsers ask for one click before sound can start.
persistent-sessions.title: Persistent sessions
persistent-sessions.1: A persistent session keeps your logins between runs, on any site that keeps you logged in when Chrome closes, with the rest of what Chrome saves but its caches: site data, history and preferences. Log in once, stop it, and when you resume it, those sites still have you logged in. What it keeps is encrypted on your server with a key only your password opens.
persistent-sessions.2: Start a session with Save this session on. Its first run starts with a fresh browser; each resume starts from what the last stop saved, and reopens the pages it had open then.
persistent-sessions.3: Stopping it saves it: Chrome closes cleanly, then its cookies, storage, history and settings are encrypted and kept. Chrome’s caches are left out; it fills them again. Chrome’s password manager stays off: it keeps what sites keep in cookies and storage, not your passwords.
persistent-sessions.4: It keeps what Chrome keeps when it closes. A login a site keeps only until the browser closes (one where you did not tick “remember me”, say) ends with the run, as it would when you quit Chrome on a desktop.
persistent-sessions.5: One run at a time: resuming it while it runs is refused until that run is stopped.
persistent-sessions.6: Agents resume only the persistent sessions you allow them: press Resume on one and choose there the tokens (and Agents on this server, the local MCP clients) that may resume it, saved as you change them. To any other, it does not exist.
persistent-sessions.7: After the server restarts, persistent sessions stay locked until you log in with your password. Signed in with a passkey, enter your password once to unlock them.
persistent-sessions.8: Each keeps up to 512 MiB. A save that cannot be made (more than that, or Chrome not closing within 20 seconds) keeps the last save, and the session says why. Stopping or updating the admin saves every persistent session that runs first, as stopping it does (up to 110 seconds in all); a run that ends any other way (a crash, the machine losing power) keeps the last save. Such a run’s saved session then says its last save could not be confirmed.
persistent-sessions.9: Up to 16 persistent sessions. Deleting one deletes what it kept for good. The public demo has none.
closing-chrome.title: Closing Chrome
closing-chrome.1: Closing Chrome’s last window, or quitting it, opens it again at the session’s first page, with the same cookies, up to 50 times per session.
starting-a-session.13: Off by default. On, whoever opens this session watches until they take control, as with a session an agent started.
chat.6: Drag the chat’s free edge to resize it, up to 70% of the window, and choose how much of the screen shows through it, up to 70%, 5% to begin with. Its place, sizes and transparency, and whether you left it open, are remembered in this browser; a session with a running chat comes back as you left it. A chat’s own files go through its own container, whatever address the admin has.
